analysis.investment_thesis: Blue Dart is India's finest express logistics brand — the DHL-backed network with 6 Boeing freighters is a genuine moat in time-sensitive B2B delivery — but a deteriorating PAT trajectory (₹382 Cr in FY22 down to ₹252 Cr in FY25) and EBITDA in contraction trend make this a declining profitability story at 44x trailing P/E, which is a combination I find very uncomfortable.
key_strengths: Best-in-class express delivery brand with unmatched air network, 35+ year track record, and sticky enterprise customer relationships
Consistent OCF generation (5/5 years positive, ₹735 Cr in FY25) — the franchise generates cash even through margin compression
DHL parentage provides technology, global connectivity, and brand credibility that new-age logistics players cannot replicate quickly
key_risks: PAT has declined every year since FY22: ₹382 → ₹371 → ₹301 → ₹252 Cr — a four-year declining profit trend in an expanding economy is alarming
Revenue CAGR of only 9.3% over 9 years is below my 12% threshold; recent growth (FY24→FY25: ₹5,268 Cr → ₹5,720 Cr) is picking up but profitability is not
Intensifying competition from Delhivery, Ekart, and XpressBees eroding pricing power in the e-commerce segment while air network costs remain fixed
red_flags: EBITDA trend is explicitly contracting — a logistics franchise where EBITDA shrinks as revenue grows signals structural cost inflation or pricing loss
Borrowings have remained stubbornly high at ₹1,000-1,100 Cr for 3+ years despite strong OCF — the debt is not being retired, suggesting working capital and lease obligations are consuming cash
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Blue Dart is a business I admire deeply — they built India's express logistics backbone before anyone else saw the opportunity. But admiring a franchise and paying 44x P/E for a business with declining profits are two very different things. The FY22 peak of ₹382 Cr PAT has eroded to ₹252 Cr in FY25 even as revenue grew from ₹4,410 Cr to ₹5,720 Cr — this tells me costs are rising faster than revenues, likely from fuel, wages, aircraft maintenance, and competitive pressure on yields.

From my perspective, a DHL subsidiary has a different alignment with minority shareholders than an owner-operated business. The promoter (DHL at 75%) makes decisions that optimise for the global network, not necessarily Indian minority shareholders. At 44x P/E, I am paying a premium for a brand and network that is losing earnings power. The forward P/E of 28x suggests analysts expect a recovery, and the e-commerce boom is a genuine tailwind for volumes — but until I see PAT recovery for two consecutive quarters, I would hold existing positions and not add fresh capital at these levels.
